concepts.title: Conditionals: if/else and switch
concepts.description: if/else chains pick exactly one branch by evaluating conditions top to bottom until the first true one wins, while switch dispatches on a single value against a set of labels -- and switch's classic fall-through behavior, together with Java's insistence on genuine boolean conditions, are two of the most consequential design decisions beginners run into.
learningObjectives: Write if/else if/else chains and explain the exact order Java evaluates them in, including which branches get skipped once a match is found.
Explain why Java requires a genuine boolean expression in an if condition, unlike languages with 'truthy' values, and what class of bug that prevents.
Use a classic switch statement correctly, including explaining fall-through behavior and why break is usually required.
Use a modern switch expression with arrow syntax and explain how it avoids fall-through by design.
Predict bugs caused by missing break statements in a switch and by ambiguous nested if/else without braces.

sections.heading: if / else if / else: Top to Bottom, First Match Wins
Java Requires a Real boolean -- No 'Truthy' Values
sections.body:
In C, `if (x)` is legal for an int x, and it's treated as true whenever x is nonzero. Many scripting languages generalize this further with 'truthy' and 'falsy' values for all sorts of types. Java deliberately does none of this: the expression inside an if must be an actual `boolean` (or `Boolean`), full stop -- `if (x)` where x is an int is a compile-time error, `incompatible types: int cannot be converted to boolean`, not a silently-accepted 'nonzero means true' shortcut.

This single restriction quietly closes off a specific, famous class of C bug. In C, `if (x = 5)` compiles -- it's an assignment expression, x is set to 5, and the expression's value (5, nonzero) is treated as true, so the branch always runs, even though the programmer almost certainly meant `==` and intended a comparison. In Java, if x is an int, the exact same typo, `if (x = 5)`, fails to compile, because the type of an assignment expression is the type of the value assigned -- here, int -- and int is not a legal if-condition type. The compiler catches the typo before the program ever runs.

It's worth being precise about the limits of this protection, though: if x is itself a `boolean`, `if (flag = true)` compiles just fine, because the assigned value's type is boolean, which is a legal condition -- and it silently overwrites flag to true while always taking the branch, reproducing the exact same category of bug in the one case where the types happen to align. Static typing closes the door for numeric and object comparisons; it doesn't provide blanket immunity for booleans specifically.

sections.heading: switch Statements: Fall-Through Is a Feature You Have to Actively Stop
Modern switch Expressions: Arrow Syntax and No Fall-Through, By Design

examples.title: The Fall-Through Bug in a Classic switch
examples.explanation: day matches case 3 exactly, so execution jumps straight to the "Wednesday" println -- but none of case 3, case 4, or default has a break statement, so control keeps falling straight through each subsequent case's code regardless of whether its label matches anything. The result is that this prints three lines -- Wednesday, Thursday, Some other day -- when a reader skimming the case 3 label alone would reasonably expect only one. This is exactly why fall-through has a reputation as one of Java's sharper edges: the code isn't broken syntactically, produces no warning, and the bug only shows up as visibly wrong runtime behavior once you actually run it and read the output carefully.

examples.title: Fixed with break, and the Modern Arrow Alternative
examples.explanation: In the classic form, adding break after each case's println stops execution from continuing into the next case the moment a match's code has finished -- day == 3 now prints only "Wednesday", exactly once, matching what a reader would naturally expect from the label alone. The arrow-based switch expression achieves the same correct result through a completely different mechanism: rather than relying on break to opt out of a default fall-through behavior, each case -> value branch is self-contained and independent by construction, so there's no shared control-flow path between cases for execution to accidentally fall into. Both versions here produce identical output for day == 3, but the arrow form makes the missing-break class of bug structurally impossible rather than merely avoided by discipline.

examples.title: if (x) Doesn't Compile for a Non-boolean x
examples.explanation: The commented-out block would fail to compile, because Java's if statement requires its condition to already be a genuine boolean expression -- there is no implicit 'nonzero counts as true' conversion the way there is in C or many scripting languages. Writing the comparison out explicitly, x != 0, produces an actual boolean, which is what if always requires. This restriction is a direct, practical benefit of static typing: an entire class of typo bugs (writing = where you meant ==, in languages that would otherwise silently accept a numeric condition) simply cannot compile in Java when the variable involved is a non-boolean type.

misconceptions.description: In a switch statement, only the matching case's code runs and then execution automatically stops there, the same way an if/else if chain stops after its first matching branch.
misconceptions.clarification: switch and if/else if behave differently here, and conflating them is exactly how fall-through bugs happen. An if/else if chain inherently runs at most one branch, by its own structure -- there's no way for two branches to both execute. A classic switch, by contrast, finds the matching case label and then keeps executing every line after it, across every subsequent case, until it hits an explicit break (or the switch ends) -- matching a label is only where execution starts, not where it's guaranteed to stop. The modern arrow-based switch expression restores the 'only one branch runs' behavior beginners expect from the classic form, but it does so by design, not by adding an implicit stop -- there's structurally no shared path for execution to fall through along.

misconceptions.description: Java's requirement that if conditions be a genuine boolean makes the classic C bug of writing = instead of == in a condition completely impossible in Java.
misconceptions.clarification: It closes the bug for numeric and object types, but not universally. if (x = 5) fails to compile when x is an int, because the assignment expression's type (int) isn't a legal condition type -- this is the protection working as intended. But if flag is already declared as a boolean, if (flag = true) compiles without complaint, because the assigned value's type is boolean, which is exactly what if requires; it silently reassigns flag to true and always takes the branch, which is the identical bug, just relocated to the one case where the types happen to line up. The rule to take away is precise: Java's type system prevents this bug whenever the variable's type isn't boolean, not whenever the variable is being used in a boolean context.

exercises.prompt: What does this print, and why?
hints: Find which case label actually matches month == 2 first, then check: does that specific case end with a break?
If a case has no break, execution keeps running the code for every case AFTER it too, regardless of whether those labels match anything.
Trace forward from case 2 until you hit the first break you actually encounter -- everything printed along the way is part of the output.
exercises.expectedAnswer:
February
March
Because case 2 has no break, execution falls through into case 3's code and stops there, since case 3 does have a break.
exercises.solutionExplanation: month == 2 matches case 2, which prints "February" -- but case 2 has no break statement, so control falls straight through into case 3's code next, printing "March" as well. case 3 does have a break, so execution stops there, and case 4 and default are never reached. The output is therefore two lines, February and March, even though only one case label actually matched the value 2 -- a direct illustration of how a single missing break can silently pull in an unrelated case's output.

exercises.prompt: This method is supposed to print exactly one line describing a traffic light color, but for "yellow" it prints two lines instead of one. Find and fix the bug.
hints: Look specifically at the case "yellow" block -- does it end with a break before moving on to the next case?
Without a break, control keeps executing into case "green"'s code too, even though the color passed in was never "green".
Add the missing break right after the 'yellow' case's println, the same way 'red' and 'green' already have one.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The case "yellow" block prints "Slow down" but has no break, so execution falls straight through into case "green"'s code next, printing "Go" as well -- even though the argument passed in was "yellow", never "green". Adding break right after the "yellow" case's println stops execution there, matching the pattern already correctly used for "red" and "green". This is the exact same category of bug switch is notorious for: the missing break produces no compiler warning and no exception, just quietly wrong extra output that's easy to miss unless you're specifically checking every case for a terminating break.

options: This fails to compile because case 1 has no break.
assessments.explanation: n matches case 1 and prints "one", but case 1 has no break, so execution falls through into case 2's code next, printing "two" as well; case 2 does have a break, so execution stops there and case 3 is never reached, giving exactly two lines: one, then two. Option A wrongly assumes execution stops automatically after a match, the way if/else if does. Option C wrongly assumes it keeps falling through past case 2's break. Option D is wrong because a case without a break is completely legal Java -- fall-through is a real, intentional language feature, not a compile error, even though it's a very common bug source.

assessments.prompt: Explain, to a beginner who is confused about why their switch statement is printing more than they expected, what fall-through actually is, why the language behaves this way, and how the modern switch expression avoids the problem entirely.
assessments.modelAnswer: In a classic Java switch statement, matching a case label is only where execution starts -- it is not, by itself, where execution stops. Once control jumps to the matching case, it keeps running every subsequent line of code, straight through the boundaries of the next case labels too, completely ignoring whether those later labels match the switched-on value at all, until it either hits an explicit break statement or reaches the very end of the switch block. This is called fall-through, and it's the reason a switch can end up printing output from cases that were never actually matched: if you forget a break at the end of a matched case's code, you get that case's output plus whatever comes immediately after it too, silently, with no compiler warning or runtime error of any kind. This isn't a mistake in the language's design so much as a deliberate original choice -- it lets several case labels intentionally share one block of code by stacking labels together with no statements in between them -- but in the vast majority of ordinary switch statements, where each case is meant to be independent, it behaves like a trap rather than a feature, and forgetting a break is an extremely common, easy-to-miss bug. Java 14 introduced switch expressions using arrow syntax (case value -> result) specifically to sidestep this: each arm is a self-contained branch that produces a value directly, with no shared control-flow path connecting it to the next case at all, so there's nothing to break out of and nothing to fall through into -- the missing-break bug becomes structurally impossible rather than merely something you have to remember to avoid.

concepts.title: Loops: for, while, and do-while
concepts.description: Java's three loop forms all repeat a block of code but differ in exactly when the condition is checked and how the iteration variable is managed -- and break, continue, and labeled loops give you fine-grained control over exactly which iteration, or which loop, gets interrupted.
learningObjectives: Trace the exact execution order of a for loop's init, condition, and update clauses across multiple iterations.
Choose between for, while, and do-while based on whether the iteration count is known ahead of time and whether the body must run at least once.
Explain precisely when do-while checks its condition relative to when while checks its, and what that changes in practice.
Use break and continue correctly, including labeled break/continue for escaping or skipping in nested loops.
Predict and diagnose an infinite loop caused by a missing or incorrect update step.
Use the enhanced for-each loop over arrays, and explain why it cannot be used to reassign an element back into a primitive array.

sections.heading: The for Loop: init, condition, update -- In That Exact Order
while and do-while: Checking Before vs Checking After
break, continue, and Labeled Loops
The Enhanced for-each Loop, and What You Give Up for the Cleaner Syntax
Infinite Loops: How They Actually Happen

examples.title: Tracing a for Loop's Exact Execution Order
examples.explanation: int i = 0 runs exactly once, before anything else. Then the sequence is: check i < 3 (true, since i is 0) -> run body, printing 'i = 0' -> run i++ , making i 1 -> check i < 3 again (true) -> print 'i = 1' -> i++ makes i 2 -> check (true) -> print 'i = 2' -> i++ makes i 3 -> check i < 3 (now false) -> loop ends without running the body again. So exactly three lines print, for i = 0, 1, and 2 -- i = 3 is checked but never printed, because the condition is evaluated before the body runs on every pass, including what would have been the fourth one.

examples.title: do-while Guarantees the Body Runs at Least Once
examples.explanation: This simulates a retry-until-valid pattern: attempt 1 and attempt 2 produce -1 (treated as invalid), so the do-while condition result < 0 keeps the loop going; attempt 3 finally produces 42, and the condition becomes false, ending the loop right after that iteration's body has already run. The key structural point is that result does not exist with any meaningful value before the first iteration -- there's nothing to check yet -- so do-while's 'run the body first, check after' order matches this pattern exactly. A plain while loop attempting the same logic would need some way to get an initial result before the loop even starts, just to have something to test against the first condition check, typically forcing you to duplicate the body's first line above the loop.

examples.title: Labeled break to Escape Nested Loops in One Step
examples.explanation: value equals target (5) when row is 1 and col is 2 (1*3 + 2 = 5). break search; exits both the inner and outer for loops in that single statement, because search is a label attached to the outer loop -- execution jumps straight to the println after the nested loops entirely, never checking row 2 at all, since there's no point once the target has already been found. Without the label, an unlabeled break here would only exit the inner loop; the outer loop would then proceed to row = 2 and needlessly run through all of its columns too, even though found is already true -- exactly the kind of wasted, easy-to-miss extra work labeled break is designed to eliminate.

misconceptions.description: continue works like a weaker version of break -- it still ends the loop, just somehow less abruptly.
misconceptions.clarification: continue does not end the loop at all. It skips only the remainder of the current iteration's body and jumps straight to the next iteration's condition check (running the update step first, in a for loop) -- the loop keeps running exactly as it otherwise would, for as many remaining iterations as its condition allows. break, by contrast, genuinely terminates the loop immediately and completely, with no further iterations of any kind. They are not two strengths of the same action; they do fundamentally different things to the loop's control flow.

misconceptions.description: In a for-each loop like for (int x : numbers), assigning a new value to x inside the loop body updates the corresponding element back in the numbers array.
misconceptions.clarification: For an array of primitive elements, x is a copy of each element, freshly created for that one iteration -- it has no ongoing connection back to the array's actual storage. Reassigning x only changes that local copy, and the array itself is completely unaffected once the loop moves to the next iteration. To actually mutate elements in place, you need the classic indexed for loop and an explicit assignment through the array itself, such as numbers[i] = newValue, which writes directly into the array's own storage rather than into a throwaway per-iteration copy.

exercises.prompt: What does this print, and why?
hints: continue at i == 2 skips only the println for that one iteration -- does the loop keep going afterward, or does it stop entirely?
break at i == 4 is a completely different action from continue -- what does it do to the rest of the loop's remaining iterations?
List out i's values in order (0,1,2,3,4) and decide, for each one, whether it reaches the println at all.
exercises.expectedAnswer:
0
1
3
i=2 hits continue and skips its println only, i=3 prints normally, and i=4 hits break and stops the loop before its println ever runs.
exercises.solutionExplanation: For i = 0 and i = 1, neither if triggers, so both print normally. For i = 2, the continue statement runs, which skips only the println below it for this one iteration and jumps straight to the loop's update step (i++) and next condition check -- the loop itself keeps going. For i = 3, again neither if triggers, so it prints normally. For i = 4, the break statement runs, which terminates the loop immediately and completely -- its println never executes, and no further iterations happen at all (i = 5 is never reached, since the loop has already ended). The final output is therefore 0, 1, 3 -- three lines, with 2 skipped by continue and 4 (and anything beyond it) cut off entirely by break.

exercises.prompt: This loop is supposed to print the numbers 5 down to 1, but it never terminates and just keeps printing forever. Find and fix the bug.
hints: For the loop to eventually stop, i > 0 has to become false at some point. What direction does i actually need to move for that to happen?
Look at the update step inside the loop body -- what operation is it actually performing on i, and does that operation move i toward or away from satisfying i > 0 being false?
The loop needs i to count DOWN toward and past 0, not up away from it.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The condition i > 0 can only ever become false if i eventually reaches 0 or goes negative -- but the original code uses i++, which increments i further away from zero on every iteration, guaranteeing i > 0 stays true forever and the loop never terminates. Changing i++ to i--, so i counts down instead of up, means i decreases by one each pass (5, 4, 3, 2, 1), and once i reaches 0, the condition i > 0 finally evaluates to false and the loop ends -- printing exactly 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 in that order, matching the intended behavior.

assessments.prompt: What is the key behavioral difference between while and do-while?
options: do-while can only be used with integers, while while works with any type.

while checks its condition before running the body on every pass, including the first, so the body might never run at all; do-while checks its condition after running the body, so the body always runs at least once.
do-while automatically breaks out after exactly one iteration, while while can run any number of times.
There is no real difference -- they are two equivalent ways of writing the same loop.
assessments.explanation: Option B correctly identifies the actual mechanism: the difference is entirely about WHEN the condition is checked relative to the body -- before every iteration for while (so a false condition up front means zero iterations), versus after the body for do-while (so the body is guaranteed to run at least once regardless of the condition's initial value). Option A is fabricated -- neither loop is restricted to integers. Option C is wrong -- do-while can run any number of iterations, just like while; it only guarantees a minimum of one. Option D is wrong because the difference described in B is a real, observable behavioral distinction, not a stylistic one -- it changes whether the body can run zero times or not.

assessments.prompt: Explain the difference between break and continue, and then explain what a labeled break adds on top of an ordinary, unlabeled one.
assessments.modelAnswer: break and continue both alter a loop's normal flow, but they do genuinely different things. break terminates the nearest enclosing loop immediately and entirely -- once it runs, no further iterations of that loop happen at all, and execution resumes at the first statement after the loop. continue is much narrower: it only skips whatever remains of the CURRENT iteration's body, then proceeds directly to the next iteration as normal -- in a for loop, that means the update step still runs and the condition is still checked again -- so the loop keeps going exactly as it otherwise would for its remaining iterations. Mixing these up is a common source of confusion, since continue is sometimes mistaken for 'a softer break,' when really it doesn't end the loop at all. A labeled break addresses a specific limitation of the plain, unlabeled version: an ordinary break, written inside a loop that's nested inside another loop, only escapes the innermost loop it's directly inside of -- the outer loop keeps running its remaining iterations untouched. By placing a label immediately before the outer loop and writing break outerLabel; inside the inner loop, you can exit both loops in one single statement, which is especially useful once you've found what you were looking for in a nested search and there's no reason to keep checking any further, in either loop. Labeled continue exists too, with the analogous meaning: skip the rest of the current iteration of the labeled (outer) loop specifically, rather than just the loop the continue statement happens to be textually inside of.

concepts.title: Methods, Overloading, and Arrays
concepts.description: A method's return type is part of its contract and must be honored on every path through its body; overloading lets several methods share a name as long as their parameter lists differ, resolved entirely at compile time; and arrays are fixed-size, reference-type containers whose 'pass a copy of the reference, not the data' behavior explains exactly which changes made inside a method survive back in the caller.
learningObjectives: Define a method with an explicit return type and explain why every reachable path through a non-void method's body must return a value.
Define overloaded methods and explain how the compiler chooses which overload to call, based on the static types of the arguments at compile time.
Predict overload-resolution behavior involving primitive widening, explaining why it's attempted before autoboxing.
Declare, initialize, and index arrays, and explain why their size is fixed once created.
Explain what is actually copied when an array is passed to a method, and why mutation through that reference is visible to the caller while reassignment of the parameter is not.
Predict and explain ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException and NullPointerException scenarios involving arrays.

sections.heading: Defining a Method: The Return Type Is a Promise the Compiler Enforces
Overloading: Same Name, Different Parameter List, Chosen at Compile Time
Overload Resolution Order: Exact Match, Then Widening, Then Autoboxing
sections.body:
When more than one overload could plausibly accept a given call, Java doesn't pick arbitrarily -- it follows a fixed preference order. It first looks for an overload matching the argument types **exactly**. If none exists, it considers **widening** a primitive to a larger compatible primitive type (`int` to `long`, `long` to `double`, and so on) -- this is attempted before **autoboxing** (wrapping a primitive in its object wrapper, like `int` into `Integer`) is even considered.

```java
static void show(long value) { System.out.println("long: " + value); }
static void show(Integer value) { System.out.println("Integer: " + value); }

show(5);   // prints "long: 5" -- widening int -> long wins over autoboxing int -> Integer
```

This often surprises people who expect the `Integer` overload to be picked because `5` 'is an int', assuming autoboxing is somehow the more natural or direct path -- but Java's resolution rules specifically prefer a same-primitive-family widening conversion over crossing into object-wrapper territory, precisely because widening was part of the language before autoboxing existed and the rule was never revisited to prefer autoboxing instead. If neither an exact match, a widening conversion, nor autoboxing produces a single unambiguous best overload, the compiler reports an ambiguity error rather than guessing.

sections.heading: Arrays: Fixed-Size, Zero-Indexed, Reference-Type Containers
Passing Arrays to Methods: What's Actually Copied

examples.title: Overload Resolution at Compile Time
examples.explanation: There are three separate methods here, all named add, distinguished only by their parameter types. When the compiler sees add(2, 3), it looks at the static types of the arguments -- two int literals -- and picks the (int, int) overload, since that's an exact match; no widening or boxing is even needed. add(2.5, 3.5) similarly matches the (double, double) overload exactly, and add("2", "3") matches the (String, String) overload -- note this last one performs string concatenation, not numeric addition, because that's what + means for the String overload's body, entirely unrelated to what + does in the other two. All of this is decided while javac is compiling the code, purely by looking at the argument types written at each call site -- none of it depends on any value that only exists while the program is running.

examples.title: Widening Beats Autoboxing in Overload Resolution
examples.explanation: 5 is an int literal, and neither overload matches int exactly -- so the compiler moves on to its fallback rules, in a fixed order: widening conversions are considered before autoboxing. Widening int to long is a same-family primitive conversion and is tried first; it succeeds, so show(long) is chosen. Autoboxing int to Integer would also technically make show(Integer) callable, but it's only ever considered if no widening conversion could satisfy the call, which isn't the case here. This often surprises people who expect Integer to win because '5 is basically an int already' -- but Java's resolution order specifically favors staying within primitive widening before ever crossing into the object-wrapper world.

examples.title: Arrays Are References: Mutation Survives a Method Call, Reassignment Doesn't
examples.explanation: mutate receives a copy of the reference stored in numbers, but that copy still points at the exact same array object -- so writing to arr[0] inside mutate writes into the one and only array that exists, and main sees the change through its own numbers variable afterward. reassign also receives a copy of that same reference, but arr = new int[]{1, 2, 3} does something different: it makes reassign's own local arr variable point at a brand-new array, without touching what numbers points at back in main at all. Once reassign returns, that new array it created is simply discarded (nothing else refers to it), and numbers in main is exactly as it was after mutate ran. The rule underneath both outcomes is the same: passing an array copies the reference, so writes through that reference are shared, but rebinding the local copy of the reference itself is not.

misconceptions.description: Overloaded methods are chosen at run time based on the actual object passed in, the same way method overriding works.
misconceptions.clarification: Overload resolution happens entirely at compile time, based on the static (declared) types of the arguments at each call site -- javac decides which overloaded method's code a given call will run, and that decision is baked into the compiled bytecode before the program ever executes. This is a fundamentally different mechanism from overriding, where a subclass provides its own version of an inherited method, and the version that actually runs is chosen at run time based on the real, actual type of the object the method is called on, not on how the reference variable is declared. Overloading is sometimes called 'compile-time polymorphism' and overriding 'run-time polymorphism' for exactly this reason -- conflating them is a common source of confusion once inheritance enters the picture.

misconceptions.description: Passing an array into a method passes a full copy of the array's contents, so changes made to it inside the method can never affect the caller's array.
misconceptions.clarification: Java passes a copy of the array's REFERENCE, not a copy of its contents -- the copied reference still points at the exact same array object the caller has. Mutating an element through that reference inside the method (arr[i] = newValue) writes into the one shared array and is visible to the caller once the method returns. What does NOT survive is reassigning the parameter variable itself (arr = new int[]{...}) -- that only repoints the method's own local copy of the reference, leaving the caller's variable pointing at the original, unaffected array. The two operations, mutating through the reference versus reassigning the reference, have opposite visibility outcomes, and it's the difference between them -- not a blanket 'arrays are always copied' or 'arrays are never copied' rule -- that actually matters.

exercises.prompt: What does this program print, and why?
hints: addPoint mutates scores[0] through the array reference it was given -- is that reference the same one main's scores variable holds?
resetScores assigns a brand-new array to its own parameter named scores -- does that reassignment reach back and change what main's scores variable points to?
Separate 'writing through the reference' (arr[i] = ...) from 'rebinding the reference itself' (arr = new int[...]) -- they have very different visibility outside the method.
exercises.expectedAnswer: 60, then 60. addPoint mutates the shared array through its reference, so the change is visible in main. resetScores only reassigns its own local copy of the parameter to a new array; main's scores variable still points at the original array, unaffected.
exercises.solutionExplanation: addPoint receives a copy of the reference stored in main's scores, but that copy points at the same underlying array -- so scores[0] = scores[0] + 10 mutates that one shared array, changing its first element from 50 to 60, which main's own scores[0] reflects immediately afterward: 60. resetScores also receives a copy of that reference, but scores = new int[scores.length] only repoints resetScores's own local parameter variable at a freshly created array full of zeros -- it does not, and cannot, change what main's scores variable points to. So after resetScores returns, main's scores is exactly as it was left by addPoint: still pointing at the original array with 60 in its first slot, giving a second printed line of 60, not 0.

exercises.prompt: This method is supposed to print every element of an array, but it throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. Find and fix the bug.
hints: For an array of length 3, what are the valid indices -- and does values.length itself ever count as a valid index?
Compare the loop's continuation condition, i <= values.length, against the actual valid index range.
Change the comparison operator so the loop stops one iteration earlier than it currently does.
exercises.solutionExplanation: For an array of length 3, the valid indices are 0, 1, and 2 -- index 3 (equal to the array's length) is one past the last real element and does not exist. The original condition, i <= values.length, allows i to reach 3, and values[3] on that final pass throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, since there is no fourth element. Changing the condition to i < values.length stops the loop after i = 2, the last valid index, which is the correct, idiomatic bound for iterating an array by index. This is the array-specific version of the same off-by-one mistake that shows up in for loops generally -- the fix is always to check the exact boundary condition against what's actually valid, rather than what looks close enough.

options: 7, because grow replaces the array data refers to with a new one.
1, because grow only reassigns its own local copy of the array reference -- it never changes what data, back in main, points to.
This throws a NullPointerException, because arr is reassigned inside grow.
0, because reassigning the parameter resets the original array's contents to their default values.
assessments.explanation: grow receives a copy of the reference stored in data, and arr = new int[]{7, 8, 9} only repoints THAT local copy at a brand-new array -- it has no way to reach back and change what main's own data variable points to, since that would require modifying the caller's variable directly, which passing a copy of a reference does not allow. So data in main still points at the original array {1, 2, 3}, completely unaffected, and data[0] prints 1. Option A describes what would happen if arrays were passed by reference to the variable itself (which Java does not do); option C is wrong because nothing here produces a null reference; option D is wrong because the original array's contents are never touched at all -- only a separate, new, and ultimately unused array is created and then discarded once grow returns.

assessments.prompt: Explain why an array passed into a method can have its elements changed by that method (visible to the caller afterward), while reassigning the array parameter itself inside that method has no effect on the caller at all. Use the concept of what is actually being copied when an argument is passed.
assessments.modelAnswer: Java is always pass-by-value, but for a reference type like an array, the 'value' being copied into the method's parameter is the reference itself -- essentially an address pointing to where the array actually lives on the heap -- not the array's contents. That copied reference still points at the exact same array object the caller has, so there are, at that point, two separate variables (the caller's and the method's parameter) both pointing at one shared array. If the method writes to an element through its reference, such as arr[0] = 99, it is writing into that one shared array object, and since the caller's variable points at that same object, the caller observes the change immediately after the method returns -- nothing needs to be 'passed back'; the caller was always looking at the same underlying data. Reassigning the parameter itself, such as arr = new int[]{1, 2, 3}, is a completely different operation: it changes what the method's own local copy of the reference points to, aiming it at a newly created array instead. That reassignment only affects the method's local variable -- it cannot reach back and change what the caller's own variable points to, because the caller's variable is a separate copy of the original reference, never connected to the method's local variable beyond having started out pointing at the same object. So the general rule is: any change made THROUGH a reference (mutating the object it points to) is visible everywhere that reference is shared, but any change made TO the reference itself (making it point elsewhere) is purely local to whichever variable was reassigned.
